label: Claude Fable 5.2
output:
Peckham
11 November 2026

Dear Kelechi,

You said put it in writing, so here it is. Paper, envelope, stamp, the whole thing. Have you seen the price of a stamp lately? I nearly sent the voice note anyway. So know that you are loved.

You asked if I was serious. I am. I think you should train as a maths teacher, and I thought so long before my birthday. I only said it out loud that night because you were on your third round of "every day is the same spreadsheet" and somebody had to change the subject.

Let me start with the bad parts, because I know you. If I only give you the nice bits, you'll decide I'm selling something and stop reading.

Teaching is hard. The marking is endless. You clear one pile and another one has grown behind it. Some days the behaviour is pure wahala, and you go home having taught nothing to anybody, wondering why you left a quiet desk where nobody argues with you about a seating plan. When I started in 2019 I cried in the car park twice in my first term. Twice, Kelechi. Sitting in my own car with the engine off, like a Nollywood film. I'm not hiding that from you. And the money: your training year will be a pay drop from what you're on now. I won't dress it up.

So that's the worst of it. You can believe the rest now.

The route I mean is the salaried one. You get paid while you train. It's one year, starting September 2027, and you're in a school the whole time, not sitting in a lecture hall. After that the pay goes up, there's a proper pension, and the holidays are real holidays. As for the car park, it got better. It gets better for everybody who stays, because you stop being new, and being new is most of what makes it hard.

Now, why you. I'm not saying this to everybody who complains about their job at my birthday. If I was, I'd have recruited half of south London by now.

You got an A in further maths, but plenty of people have that and can't explain a thing. What I remember is Moremi before exams. Half the hostel was waiting for you with past questions, and you'd go through the same thing four different ways until it landed. Nobody left feeling stupid. You're patient and you're funny, and you explain things without making people feel small. I work with trained teachers who still can't do that.

And don't tell me that was Unilag and you've lost it. Christmas. My nephew, fractions, the jollof rice. You had that boy dividing portions onto plates and arguing about who got three eighths. He still talks about it. I teach fractions for a living and no child has ever gone home talking about my lesson the way he talks about your rice.

Let me tell you about last month. I have a Year 11 boy, Damola. We had been fighting simultaneous equations for three weeks. Three weeks of him looking at me like I was speaking Latin. Then one Tuesday it just went in. He looked at his page, looked at me, and shouted "Is that all??" The whole class clapped. For maths, Kelechi! I've been doing this job seven years and I thought about that boy all the way home.

When last did somebody clap at your spreadsheet?

I'm not insulting quantity surveying. Somebody has to check the costings. I just don't think it has to be you, for another nine years, when you could be standing in front of thirty children doing the thing you're actually best at. You're wasting yourself, and I say it with love and a little bit of irritation.

Here is the other thing. Our school has 1,100 kids, and since September two of our Year 9 maths groups have been taught by a supply teacher. Two classes of thirteen-year-olds, right at the age when they decide whether maths is for them or not, and we can't find a permanent maths teacher to put in front of them. That's the situation all over. So this is not charity work for a bored surveyor. Schools need exactly what you have.

And before you start with "I'm 34, I'm too old to be starting again": a woman in my department started at 41. She's very good, and nobody has ever asked her what took so long. You'd qualify with years to spare.

Which brings me to your own mouth. On your last birthday you said, and I quote, "I just want to do something that matters before 40." I didn't forget. You know I don't forget things. I'm holding you to it the same way you held me to this letter.

So here is what I'm asking. I'm not asking you to resign or to apply. I'm not asking you to sign anything at all.

There is an open evening on Thursday 19 November, 6pm, at the training partnership in Lewisham. It's the people who actually run the salaried route, so you can ask them every awkward question you like about money and hours and what the year looks like. Applications for September 2027 open soon, which is why I'm chasing you now and not in January. I'll come with you. You sit there, you listen, you interrogate them the way you interrogate a contractor's invoice, and afterwards you tell me what you think.

If you come out and say "no, this is not for me," fine. I'll leave it alone, and you can go back to your spreadsheet with my blessing and complain at my next birthday as usual. But I don't think that's what you'll say. I think you'll sit in that room and remember Moremi.

It's one evening, Kelechi. You've sat through longer meetings about concrete.

You said you'd read this on the train, so by now you're somewhere on the line pretending not to smile. I can see you. Reply however you like. Voice note is fine. I'm not as strict as you.

19 November. 6pm. Lewisham. Put it in your phone before your stop.

Your friend since Moremi,

---

I left the sign-off blank for you to sign by hand. I guessed class sizes of about thirty and said "one Tuesday" for Damola's breakthrough, so change those if they're off.
